duplicate.A: Both issues show the same failure: a stale Claude AppX container job/silo, 0x80070020 at job conversion (events 215/208), cured by logoff or reboot. But #53247 blames an app crash during startup, while #73107 is an upgrade where orphaned (elevated) children keep the old version's container alive. Commenters add further holders (CoworkVMService, adb, tail.exe). They probably share a fix (terminate the container's remaining processes), but the triggers differ enough that I can't be confident.
duplicate.B: Both issues have the same signature: AppModel-Runtime 215/208 with 0x80070020 at job-to-silo conversion, a stale Claude container job, and recovery only by reboot or logoff. #73107 finds the cause: leftover processes keep the old container job alive. Cleaning up the container job on teardown or launch would fix both. #53247 suspects a startup crash, but it also found no file lock, which fits this mechanism, and #53247 is still open.

summary: /fork <prompt> also delivers the prompt to the parent session as a user message, so the parent runs the same task, which can duplicate outward actions.
evidence: Confirmed on 2.1.217. A September comment shows the /fork command-args land as a user message in the parent. /fork was reworked in 2.1.212, 2.1.221 and 2.1.257, but no line fixes the args leaking to the parent.
next_action: Reproduce on the latest build; if it still happens, mark the /fork args in the parent as non-actionable (system note) instead of a user message.
security_why: Outward actions such as issues, PRs or messages can run twice.

security.A: The user did ask for the task. The parent running it a second time is a functional bug: duplicate tool runs and possibly duplicate public actions. It is not a permission bypass, an action the user denied, or data loss. Since 2.1.221, forks get their own worktree, so the shared-checkout race is also gone. Treat it as a normal bug, not a security issue.
security.B: The parent session's duplicate actions still go through the user's normal permission mode and prompts. In the reported case, nothing was destroyed and no duplicate was actually filed. 2.1.221 gave forks their own worktree, which removes the shared-checkout race. What remains is a real bug (the command-args land as a user message in the parent) that risks duplicate outward actions and wastes tokens, which is closer to S3 than to a medium-severity destructive action.

title: /fork <prompt> leaks the forked task into the parent session — the parent executes it too (risking duplicate side effects)

summary: With concurrent sessions in sibling worktrees, the Bash tool's cwd silently moves into another worktree, so git commands such as reset run in the wrong tree.

security.A: The cwd moved into a sibling worktree with no `cd` issued, and a `git reset --soft` ran in the wrong tree and moved the sibling's branch ref (restored from the reflog). The same drift with `--hard` or `checkout` would destroy uncommitted work, and no changelog line fixes it. A destructive-action rating at S1 is defensible.
security.B: The cwd moved into a sibling worktree without any cd, and a git reset --soft then ran in the wrong tree and moved the sibling's branch ref, which had to be restored from the reflog. Commands like --hard or checkout from the same drifted directory could silently destroy uncommitted work, so S1 is reasonable for a harness defect.

summary: ExitWorktree remove and isolation:worktree cleanup silently remove worktrees whose submodule clones hold stashes or unpushed commits, leaving that work to be pruned.
evidence: 2.1.274 'Improved safety checks before removing an agent worktree that contains submodule checkouts' covers only uncommitted files; the reporter shows that stashes and commits on other branches are still missed on 2.1.318. Labeled data-loss.
next_action: Route to the worktree tools owners: before removing, check submodule clones for stashes and for commits not on any remote-tracking ref.
security_why: Unpushed submodule work becomes orphaned and is deleted by the next worktree prune or gc.

security.A: The detailed repro shows that stashes and commits on other branches held only in a worktree's submodule clone are removed with no warning on 2.1.318. The leftover clone is then orphaned and deleted by worktree prune or gc. 2.1.274 ('Improved safety checks before removing an agent worktree that contains submodule checkouts') only catches uncommitted files. The loss is delayed and needs submodules inside worktrees, so S1 rather than S0 is right.
security.B: The reporter's repro shows stashes and unpushed commits in submodule clones removed with no warning on 2.1.318, after the 2.1.274 'Improved safety checks before removing an agent worktree that contains submodule checkouts'. The work is orphaned and deleted by the next `git worktree prune` or gc. It can only be recovered by hand, which counts as work-loss severity. The deletion isn't immediate, but that doesn't make S1 overstated.

title: [BUG] Worktree cleanup silently removes worktrees whose submodule clones hold stashes or unpushed commits
